I searched for 7 CFR 273.10(e)(2)(iii). The short version: that paragraph only covers households of three or more people. The minimum-benefit rule for one- and two-person households is in a different paragraph, (e)(2)(ii)(C). Because categorically eligible households don't have to pass the net income test, a categorically eligible one- or two-person household gets the minimum benefit even when its net income is above the normal limit.

## What §273.10(e)(2)(iii) says
It applies to an eligible household with three or more members which is entitled to no benefits (except because of the proration requirements of paragraph (a)(1) and the provision precluding issuances of less than $10 in an initial month of paragraph (e)(2)(ii)(B)). For these households, the State agency shall deny the household's application on the grounds that its net income exceeds the level at which benefits are issued. The alternative under (B) appears to be that the State agency shall certify the household but suspend its participation, subject to the following conditions.

## The minimum benefit for one- and two-person households: §273.10(e)(2)(ii)(C)
- Except during an initial month, all eligible one-person and two-person households shall receive minimum monthly allotments equal to the minimum benefit. The minimum benefit is 8 percent of the maximum allotment for a household of one, rounded to the nearest whole dollar.
- The categorical eligibility rules point back to this paragraph: All eligible households of one or two persons must be provided the minimum benefit, as required by § 273.10(e)(2)(ii)(C).
- The base benefit formula in (e)(2)(ii)(A) lists (e)(2)(iii) as an exception: Except as provided in paragraphs (a)(1), (e)(2)(iii) and (e)(2)(vi) of this section, the household's monthly allotment shall be equal to the maximum SNAP allotment for the household's size reduced by 30 percent of the household's net monthly income.

## Why categorically eligible households can be over the net income limit
- Under §273.9(a), households which are categorically eligible as defined in § 273.2(j)(2) or 273.2(j)(4) do not have to meet either the gross or net income eligibility standards.
- The Congressional Research Service puts it this way: it is possible to be categorically eligible for SNAP but have net income too high to actually receive a benefit. The exception to this is one- or two-person households that would still receive the minimum benefit.
- State manuals say the same thing. Nebraska's: Eligible one or two-person households whose income exceeds the net income limits are entitled to the minimum monthly benefit. Georgia's: One and Two Person households that are categorically eligible will be eligible for at least $24, even if the tables do not show a benefit amount at their net income levels.

## Exceptions to the minimum benefit
- **Initial month:** If the calculation of benefits in accordance with paragraph (e)(2)(ii)(A) of this section for an initial month would yield an allotment of less than $10 for the household, no benefits shall be issued to the household for the initial month.
- **National benefit reductions:** In the event that the national reduction in benefits is 90 percent or more of the benefits projected to be issued for the affected month, the provision for a minimum benefit for households with one or two members only may be disregarded.
- **Suspensions or cancellations:** The provision for the minimum benefit for households with one or two members only shall be disregarded and all households shall have their benefits suspended or cancelled for the designated month.

## Current amounts
- For FY2026, the minimum benefit was $24 in fiscal year 2026 for 48 states and the District of Columbia (with higher amounts for Alaska, Hawai'i, Guam, and the Virgin Islands).
- Some state materials published in the last few days use $25. Oklahoma says all categorically eligible households with one or two household members, including households categorically eligible due to Oklahoma 2-1-1, qualify for the minimum allotment of $25. Massachusetts Legal Help also lists Minimum benefit level for 1- and 2-person households is $25. That probably reflects the FY2027 figure, which starts October 1, 2026, but check it against the official USDA FNS cost-of-living adjustment memo.

## Categorical Eligibility Exception
"Households which are categorically eligible as defined in § 273.2(j)(2) or 273.2(j)(4) do not have to meet either the gross or net income eligibility standards."

The regulation includes as unearned income: "Support or alimony payments made directly to the household from nonhousehold members" and various assistance payments, pensions, and benefits.

"Any income in the certification period which is received too infrequently or irregularly to be reasonably anticipated, but not in excess of $30 in a quarter" may be excluded.

Educational assistance qualifies for exclusion when it's "Awarded to a household member enrolled at a recognized institution of post-secondary education" and used for allowable expenses like tuition, fees, books, and transportation—though "Normal living expenses which are room and board are not excludable."

## Loan Treatment
"All loans, including loans from private individuals as well as commercial institutions, other than educational loans on which repayment is deferred" are excluded from income.

The medical expense deduction applies to "any household member who is elderly or disabled" and covers "That portion of medical expenses in excess of $35 per month."

# Key Provisions on SNAP Benefit Calculations

## Minimum Benefits for Small Households

Paragraph (e)(2)(ii)(C) states: "all eligible one-person and two-person households shall receive minimum monthly allotments equal to the minimum benefit."

The regulation defines this minimum as "8 percent of the maximum allotment for a household of one, rounded to the nearest whole dollar."

## Benefits When Net Income Exceeds Threshold

Under (e)(2)(iii), when a three-or-more-member household's net income is too high to generate any benefits, states may either deny the application or certify the household in suspended status, allowing conversion to active benefits when circumstances change.

## Core Income Calculation Steps

Paragraph (e)(1)(i) requires states to:

1. Calculate total gross income by adding earned and unearned income, then subtracting exclusions
2. Apply the "earned income deduction" by multiplying earned income by 20 percent and subtracting that amount
3. Subtract the "standard deduction" (a set amount based on household size)
4. Deduct allowable medical expenses exceeding $35
5. Subtract dependent care and other permitted expenses
6. Calculate excess shelter costs

These deductions reduce gross income to determine the net monthly income figure used for eligibility and benefit determinations.

I found the official Texas Works Handbook sections, B-470 and A-1340, along with several secondary guides. In short, a Texas household is categorically eligible for SNAP if everyone in it gets TANF or SSI, or if it meets the TANF non-cash resource rule and has gross income at or below 165% of the federal poverty level.

## The handbook rule (Section B-471)
A SNAP household is categorically eligible if either:
- all members are approved for TANF cash assistance or SSI; or the household meets the resource criteria to be authorized to receive TANF Non-cash (TANF-NC) services (see A-1210, General Policy); and has gross income less than or equal to 165 percent of the Federal Poverty Income Limit (FPIL) for its size.

Things to know:
- For TANF-NC, a household is not categorically eligible if one or more members has a current SNAP IPV disqualification. (IPV means an intentional program violation.)
- If the household meets the combined resource limit of $5,000 for liquid assets and excess vehicle value, the household is still authorized to receive TANF-NC, and their remaining resources are exempt.
- Categorically eligible households are subject to fewer eligibility requirements than other SNAP households. However, categorical eligibility does not mean the applicants automatically receive SNAP.

## Section B-472: what households on TANF or SSI skip
Categorically eligible households are not subject to the resource and gross or net income limits. These households are exempt from verification requirements for: Social Security numbers (SSNs); resources; residence; and sponsored alien information.

## Section A-1340: the income tests
- **Gross income test:** This test applies to all households except those with a member who is elderly or has a disability, or that are categorically eligible. A household subject to the gross income test is ineligible if unrounded gross income exceeds the limit by one cent or more.
- **Net income test:** This test applies to all households, except categorically eligible households.
- **Elderly or disabled exception:** The net income test applies to a household with a member who is elderly or has a disability if the household's gross income exceeds 165 percent FPL and the household does not meet categorically eligible requirements.

## Dollar limits for FY 2026 (Oct. 1, 2025 – Sept. 30, 2026)
A secondary source lists these monthly 165% limits: 1 person $2,152; 2 people $2,909; 3 people $3,665; 4 people $4,421; 5 people $5,177; 6 people $5,934; 7 people $6,690; 8 people $7,446; each additional person +$757. The regular federal limits are 130% for gross income ($1,696 for one person) and 100% for net income.

**These numbers are already out of date.** A new federal fiscal year started on October 1, 2026, and the limits are updated each year. One screener tool shows figures for Oct. 1, 2026 through Sept. 30, 2027, for example 5 people $5319 / month, 6 people $6100 / month, 7 people $6880 / month, each additional person +$782 / month. Another guide puts a single person at roughly $2,195 per month. I couldn't find official HHSC tables for this new year, so check the current Texas Works Handbook income charts before relying on any figure.

## Who doesn't qualify this way
- According to one guide, if your household includes someone disqualified from SNAP for an intentional program violation or a primary wage earner who quit a job without good cause, the standard 130% gross income and 100% net income federal tests apply instead of the higher Texas threshold.
- Another notes that Texas uses the 165% figures for categorically eligible households and for the special elderly or disabled separate-household test. Other households may be subject to the regular 130% gross and 100% net tests.
- Even if a household passes the 165% gross test, the benefit amount still depends on net income after deductions.

One small inconsistency: one guide lists slightly different FY 2026 figures for 2 and 3 people ($2,904 and $3,660) than the other sources ($2,909 and $3,665).

**Educational assistance is exempt income for all programs, including SNAP (A-1322.1)**
- Educational assistance, including educational loans, scholarships, fellowships, grant monies, and work study, are exempt, regardless of the source.
- Loans for education, including loans from relatives or other people, are considered as educational assistance only if payment is deferred.

- **A-1326.2.1, Child support:** For SNAP, child support counts as unearned income.

**About the memo**
- The memo is dated August 13, 2025 and sent to all SNAP State Agencies. It provides the fiscal year (FY) 2026 Cost-of-Living Adjustments (COLA) to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) maximum allotments, income eligibility standards, and deductions.
- In accordance with the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008, the COLAs are effective as of October 1, 2025.

**Minimum benefit**
- The memo says the minimum benefit for the 48 States and D.C. will increase to $24. It applies from October 1, 2025, to September 30, 2026, for households of 1–2 people.
- The minimum is higher outside the 48 states and D.C.: Alaska ($31-$48 depending on region), Hawaii ($41), Guam ($35), and the U.S. Virgin Islands ($31).
- This was a $1 increase. The minimum had sat flat at $23 for three straight years (FY2023-FY2025).
- Benefits are calculated if the math produces anything above $0, you get at least the minimum; if it produces $0 or below, you're not approved. Households of 3 or more have no minimum: if the formula yields less than $24 they receive that smaller computed amount.

**Other FY 2026 figures in the memo**
- The maximum allotment for a family of four in the 48 States and D.C., will be $994. For one person, the FY2026 maximum is $298.
- Maximum allotments for a family of four will range from $1,285 to $1,995 in Alaska. The maximum allotment for a family of four in Hawaii will decrease to $1,689.
- The shelter cap value will increase to $744 for the 48 States and D.C.
- The standard deduction for household sizes 1 through 3 increased to $209 a month for the 48 states and D.C.
- The maximum homeless shelter deduction will increase to $198.99 in all areas.
- The asset limits didn't change: $3,000 for most households and $4,500 for households with a member who is 60 or older or disabled.

**These figures are now out of date**
Today is October 6, 2026, so FY 2027 has started and the FY 2026 numbers ended September 30, 2026. Some third-party sites report that the minimum SNAP benefit for eligible one- and two-person households is $24 in FY 2026. It increases to $25 in FY 2027 for the 48 states and D.C. One of them also says the asset limit for households with an elderly or disabled member climbed to $4,750. I didn't find the official USDA FY 2027 memo, so check these numbers against the USDA Food and Nutrition Service before relying on them.
